title: All-Time Great Indian Social Films
description: 25 landmark Indian films that confronted caste, inequality, gender, poverty, discrimination, education and injustice while holding a mirror to Indian society.

entries.why_it_ranks: Bimal Roy's devastating portrait of a farmer losing his land brought poverty, exploitation and rural displacement to the centre of Indian cinema.
Kamal Haasan and Madhavan carry a profoundly human film about compassion, class, ideology, faith and what it actually means to be a good human being.
Satyajit Ray transformed the everyday struggles of a poor rural family into universal cinema without reducing poverty to melodrama.
A mainstream investigative drama that forces caste discrimination and institutional inequality directly into the conversation.
A powerful legal drama about custodial violence and the persecution of marginalized tribal communities, anchored by an exceptionally affecting story.
Nagraj Manjule examines caste through a young boy's first love and humiliation, culminating in one of modern Indian cinema's most powerful endings.
Chaitanya Tamhane quietly exposes how bureaucracy, class and institutional indifference operate inside the justice system.
Mari Selvaraj confronts caste violence through education, friendship, love and the everyday humiliations endured by its protagonist.
Beyond its epic stature, the film examines rural poverty, debt, exploitation, motherhood and the moral expectations imposed on ordinary people.
Its central argument — that consent cannot be overridden by assumptions about a woman's clothes, lifestyle or relationships — entered mainstream popular discourse.
A heartbreaking examination of how social expectations, reputation and circumstances can gradually destroy an ordinary young man's future.
Pa. Ranjith uses land ownership, caste, housing and political power to examine who truly has the right to a city.
Caste, sexual morality, grief and social judgment intersect beautifully through parallel stories set in Varanasi.
What begins as an exhilarating romance ultimately becomes one of contemporary Indian cinema's most devastating examinations of caste.
A young woman pursuing cricket becomes the centre of a story about gender barriers, farming distress, family and ambition.
Historically essential for confronting untouchability and caste barriers through tragic romance at an extraordinarily early stage of Indian sound cinema.
Bimal Roy examines untouchability, prejudice and supposedly progressive middle-class attitudes through an intimate human story.
A tiny theft opens up questions about poverty, policing, morality and how differently institutions treat ordinary people.
Two children simply wanting to taste pizza becomes a funny and poignant examination of poverty, consumerism and class aspiration.
Beneath its family drama is a thoughtful examination of masculinity, dysfunctional families, gender expectations and alternative ideas of what makes a home.
A hugely accessible mainstream film about women challenging entrenched gender expectations through sport.
Ram uses the relationship between a father and his daughter to explore disability, sexuality, caregiving and society's discomfort with people who do not fit its expectations.
Everyday household routines become an extraordinarily effective critique of patriarchy, unpaid domestic labour and gender roles.
Multiple relationships across age, religion, caste and social status create an unusually compassionate portrait of ordinary Indian lives.
A seemingly simple school story gradually exposes childhood hunger, dignity and the cruelty adults can unknowingly — or knowingly — inflict on children.
